significance.justification: A verified-true result would license the form-(iii) conclusion that editing a load-bearing representation of a scientific variable produces an output-response curve matching the relevant scientific law in sign and magnitude, while most merely decodable concepts have low "mechanistic fidelity"; this fixes a family of counterfactual responses rather than one isolated behavior. It would establish both a phenomenon—"a minority of decodable scientific concepts pass"—and a causal mechanism connecting an internal variable to lawful downstream computation, addressing the decodability-versus-use distinction underlying Hewitt and Liang's 2019 control-task critique and Geiger et al.'s causal-abstraction work. A negative result in which decodable variables generally do realize the predicted curves would still reject the spectator-encoding explanation, although the aggregate words "many" and "minority" lack a precise threshold; the per-concept true and false states are nevertheless distinguishable. In the topic-substitution check, the generic scientific-representation topic alone would not imply quantitative counterfactual curve matching or widespread spectator encoding, so the score derives from the claim-specific law rather than the topic.

reach.justification: The named handle is the "mechanistic fidelity" score, defined as "the fraction of predicted counterfactual variance realized," which downstream researchers could use as a diagnostic for whether a decoded concept participates in a claimed mechanism. It is principally post hoc: the score is obtained after editing a representation and observing its downstream effect, and the claim does not explicitly provide advance warning of deployment failures or another action window. Although the hypothesis asserts applicability "Across scientific foundation models" and several scientific domains, re-extraction on a new model does not predict which concepts will pass—only the conditional response expected if they are load-bearing—so the main transferable asset is an auditing procedure and normalized metric for interpretability researchers rather than a forecast for model builders or deployers. The topic-substitution check lowers this from the broad-reach bands: the scientific-representation topic alone would suggest cross-domain relevance, whereas the claim-specific handle supports useful but mostly research-facing, post-hoc uptake.
